title: Four ways to unstage, one of which destroys your work
summary: reset, reset --hard, restore --staged and rm --cached all 'unstage' something. Run each one and watch precisely which of the three areas it touches.
mental_model: Every one of these commands answers 'which areas do I overwrite?'. `restore --staged` and `reset` touch the index only. `reset --hard` touches the index AND the working tree. That single difference is the whole risk.
danger: `git reset --hard` overwrites your files. Anything not committed is gone, with no reflog entry to recover it.

steps.title: Stage three changes plus a new file
steps.why: Four things in the index, each of which we will remove differently. Keep an eye on the file contents, not just the status letters.
steps.expect: Three M and one A, all in the left column.

steps.title: restore --staged — the clear spelling
steps.why: It copies HEAD's version into the index. The working tree is not mentioned in the command and not touched by it: a.py on disk still says 99.
steps.expect: a.py moves to the right column and still reads 99.

steps.title: reset — the older spelling, same effect
steps.why: `git reset <path>` is `--mixed` by default: index updated, working tree left alone. Identical outcome to restore --staged, which is why the newer command exists.
steps.expect: b.py behaves exactly like a.py did.

steps.title: rm --cached — unstages a NEW file completely
steps.why: For a file that was never in HEAD, there is no old version to restore. `rm --cached` drops it from the index entirely and it reverts to untracked — still on disk.
steps.expect: new.py becomes ?? untracked, and the file survives.

steps.title: reset --hard — the one that takes your edits with it
steps.why: This resets index AND working tree to HEAD. c.py loses its 99 permanently. Notice the other files: a.py and b.py lose their edits too, because --hard is repo-wide, not path-scoped.
steps.expect: All three back to 1. Only untracked new.py survives.

verify.label: reset --hard reverted the working tree too

steps.title: Confirm what survived and what did not
steps.why: Untracked files are outside reset's remit — that is why new.py is still here. Committed history is untouched. Only uncommitted tracked edits were destroyed.

verify.label: the new file ended up untracked, not staged
reset --hard reverted every tracked edit
verify.hint: that is the point — --hard is repo-wide and destructive

verify.label: history was never at risk — only uncommitted work was

pitfalls: `git reset --hard` takes no path argument in the form people expect. It resets everything, not just the file you were thinking about.
`git reset <path>` and `git restore --staged <path>` are equivalent. Prefer restore: reset does four different jobs depending on flags.
Unstaging a never-committed file needs `rm --cached`; `restore --staged` on it silently does nothing useful.
If you are about to run --hard and are not certain, run `git stash -u` instead. Same clean tree, fully reversible.
cheatsheet: unstage a file that was never committed
index AND working tree back to HEAD — destructive
undo a commit, keep everything staged
the reversible way to get a clean tree
